name: Falcon
intro: This is the bottom half of Falcon, which landed Dave Scott and Jim Irwin near Hadley Rille on 30 July 1971. It carried the first Moon car folded against its side, and the crew lived in it for almost three days. When they left, it stayed behind as their launch pad.

hotspots.title: Hammer and feather
hotspots.text: Beside Falcon, Dave Scott dropped a hammer and a feather at the same moment. With no air to slow the feather, they hit the ground together, just as Galileo had predicted.

video.caption: Dave Scott holds up a hammer and a feather, lets go, and both land at the same time.

video.audio: Real radio from the Moon: Dave Scott explains the test (“in my left hand, I have a feather; in my right hand, a hammer”) and reacts as they land.

hotspots.title: Climbing down
hotspots.text: Scott and Irwin climbed down this ladder for three moonwalks. Together they collected 77 kg of rock, including a piece of ancient crust nicknamed the Genesis Rock.

hotspots.title: Where the rover rode
hotspots.text: The first Moon car rode folded up against the side of Falcon. Irwin climbed up and pulled a lanyard, and it unfolded onto the ground.

source.label: Apollo Lunar Surface Journal: Apollo 15 video library

photo.alt: The gold-foil-wrapped lunar module stands on grey ground in front of a big rounded mountain.
photo.caption: Falcon early on the first moonwalk, with the mountain Hadley Delta behind.
photo.licenseEvidence: NASA Image and Video Library item as15-086-11600 (JSC); no third-party credit or copyright notice on the item. NASA: images and video "generally are not subject to copyright in the United States" (https://www.nasa.gov/nasa-brand-center/images-and-media/).

hotspots.title: The landing engine
hotspots.text: This engine slowed Falcon down for a landing at the foot of the Apennine Mountains, beside a winding valley called Hadley Rille.

hotspots.title: The missing top half
hotspots.text: The cabin sat here until 2 August 1971, when it blasted off while the rover’s TV camera broadcast the launch live to Earth.

video.caption: The rover's TV camera, steered from Houston by Ed Fendell, watches the top half of the lunar module Falcon blast off from the Moon on 2 August 1971.

funFact: The feather Dave Scott dropped was a falcon feather, chosen for their lander, Falcon.
whyLeft: Nothing broke: the bottom half was always meant to stay as a launch pad for the crew’s cabin.
repurpose: Its engine is spent, but its gold foil and metal are a record of 50 years on the Moon that future visitors could photograph without touching.
